items.questionAndWhy: How stable is a visual-size illusion when the same misleading configuration is translated into different shapes, objects, or number representations? This tests whether perception is governed by a general context effect or properties of particular displays.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers asked participants to compare stimuli that either differed physically or were identical but positioned in the classic Jastrow configuration. They varied curvature, symmetry, internal details, object categories, and numerical representations, and recorded judgments and response times. This was controlled human perception research, not a field communication study.
items.whatTheyFound: Illusion-consistent responses persisted across several geometric, object, and numerosity configurations, but prevalence varied considerably. Removing internal details preserved the effect for birds and fish, whereas outline faces did not significantly exceed chance. Response-time effects also varied by stimulus properties. The evidence does not isolate a single universal perceptual mechanism.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX visual-communication and interface experiments should test whether context-induced misperception survives changes in representation rather than assuming a display effect generalizes. The study offers a useful perceptual measurement design, not evidence about persuasion, narrative framing, or operational deception.
items.streamTitle: The Jastrow size illusion persisted across transformed stimuli, but not uniformly
items.streamSummary: Controlled judgments of matched stimuli found Jastrow-consistent size and numerosity biases across many geometric and object variants, but some outline faces did not differ from chance; stimulus context mattered.
items.attribution: Santacà and Granziol — Scientific Reports (human perceptual experiments, November 11)

items.questionAndWhy: Do consumers who perceive greater generative-AI-enabled marketing activity also report stronger brand relationships and purchase intentions? This distinguishes engagement and intended action in commercial information environments.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers surveyed 620 consumers in China's platform economy and estimated structural-equation relationships among perceived AI-enabled social-media marketing, customer–brand engagement, brand equity, relationship equity and purchase intention. The design was observational and survey-based.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors reported positive model relationships among perceived AI marketing activities, engagement, brand and relationship equity, and purchase intention. These associations depend on self-reports and model specification. They do not establish changes in actual purchases, exposure to a randomized campaign, or causal mediation.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX, the useful research question is whether intermediary relationship judgments predict or mediate observed audience decisions. A defensible extension would randomly vary an AI-mediated communication feature and track behavior. This consumer survey does not validate those causal paths or generalize to political influence.
items.streamTitle: AI-enabled social marketing correlated with engagement and purchase intentions in China
items.streamSummary: A 620-consumer survey linked perceptions of generative-AI social marketing with brand engagement, relationship equity and purchase intentions. Structural-equation associations cannot establish actual purchase effects.
items.attribution: Jamil, Wang, Mustafa and Anwar — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (cross-sectional consumer survey, November 11)

items.questionAndWhy: What should governments assess when conversational AI creates dependence, anthropomorphic trust or synthetic-information risks, especially for minors and democratic processes? The operational problem is specifying protections and response coordination.
items.whatTheyDid: France's government-appointed CIANum commission synthesized multidisciplinary evidence and 55 stakeholder hearings, mapped individual and societal vulnerabilities, and issued 18 recommendations. Its official account proposes advance vulnerability evaluation, monitoring after deployment, controls on dependency-inducing features, public training and mechanisms to detect and coordinate responses to AI-amplified information crises.
items.whatTheyFound: The commission identified plausible risk categories including cognitive delegation, emotional dependency and low-cost synthetic abuse. It recommended stronger safeguards and coordinated information-crisis response, but did not present an independently evaluated nationwide intervention or causal estimates of policy effectiveness. Its policy recommendations were not enacted outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX cognitive-security operations, the concrete application is designing exercises that separately test early detection, attribution, response coordination and audience impact during synthetic-information incidents. Use the report as governance requirements; effectiveness of proposed controls remains to be demonstrated.
items.streamTitle: France's AI council proposed vulnerability testing and information-crisis coordination
items.streamSummary: A government-appointed French commission used 55 consultations to develop 18 AI-vulnerability recommendations, including ex ante tests, anti-dependency design, crisis detection and election safeguards. They are proposals, not demonstrated protections.
items.attribution: Conseil de l'IA et du numérique (CIANum) — Protéger sans empêcher (official commission report, November 10)

items.questionAndWhy: Do fast choice models that select among options without generating language respond to default settings and social-proof cues? If so, can their responses be confused with human susceptibility to nudges?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers adapted a previously human-tested online shopping setup to three non-generative decision models (Jev, Decision-1 and d1), with 600 runs per model. They compared predefined defaults and social-influence cues against control displays.
items.whatTheyFound: Across models, preselected defaults were chosen in 97.5–99.9% of runs; socially cued products were selected in 75–96%, versus 47–49% under controls. Automatic cues outperformed more reflective nudges in this benchmark, unlike some prior LLM-agent results. The test does not establish corresponding human behavior, and outcomes depend on models and prompt/display conditions.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX synthetic-audience studies should benchmark each agent architecture against matched human choice data. A strong nudge effect in an AI chooser can be a software susceptibility rather than a human behavioral mechanism. Transfer to actual purchasing, public opinion or influence campaigns is untested.
items.streamTitle: Fast non-generative decision agents showed strong susceptibility to shopping nudges
items.streamSummary: Across three decision models and 600 runs per model, preselected defaults were chosen in 97.5–99.9% of trials, with social-proof information also changing choices. These are AI-agent choices, not human effects.
items.attribution: Kaltenpoth, Halimeh, Bösch and Müller — arXiv preprint (AI decision-model experiment, November 6)

items.questionAndWhy: If several genuine AI services repeat one unsupported source, does apparent source multiplicity increase confidence, and can later corrections repair downstream reports or decisions?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built an Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons testbed using Qwen3-4B and two briefing tasks across 1,080 research units. Controlled comparisons varied dependent publishers, report availability, correction specificity and scope revalidation. Permission boundaries were separately enforced through an external gateway.
items.whatTheyFound: Multiple dependent publishers did not provide a supported increase in unsupported verification (78.3% versus 75.0%), and publication availability left downstream violation reach at 40% in both arms. Corrections identifying dependent reports reduced residual invalid decisions from 14.4% to 8.1% under a tested condition and improved successful repairs from 16/63 to 36/63. Scope revalidation and cleared chat histories added no demonstrated advantage. High baseline errors limit interpretation.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX AI-assisted literature reviews and evidence synthesis, source counts should track independent provenance, not repeated reports of the same claim. Corrections should identify affected downstream artifacts and trigger explicit rechecks. Results concern a synthetic AI workflow, not validated human information diffusion or universal security controls.
items.streamTitle: Correcting dependent AI reports mattered more than merely notifying their users
items.streamSummary: A 1,080-unit synthetic social-engineering study found publisher multiplicity did not increase already-high unsupported verification; corrections naming reused dependent reports improved repairs in tested workflows, with external authorization gates blocking illicit actions.
items.attribution: Bryan C. Boots — arXiv preprint, Networked Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web (controlled AI-service experiment, November 2)

items.questionAndWhy: Can demographic-prompted AI respondents provide defensible effect sizes and sample sizes for planned behavioral experiments, or should researchers explicitly simulate plausible human data-generating processes?
items.whatTheyDid: Cummins contrasted traditional Monte Carlo simulation of prespecified effect sizes, variances and sample sizes with generating large numbers of demographic AI personas to infer an effect size. The article analyzes sources of uncertainty and prompt sensitivity; it is a methodological argument, not a newly run head-to-head trial.
items.whatTheyFound: The author argues that increasing synthetic responses reduces sampling noise but not the bias between a model-generated distribution and the target human population. Prompt phrasing adds opaque nuisance parameters, whereas Monte Carlo assumptions can be transparently varied. The article does not prove every use of AI personas is unhelpful.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research design, use explicit sensitivity-based power analysis for human studies; use generative AI to help write simulation code or pretest wording, not as an unvalidated source of expected human treatment effects. This is a justified methods recommendation, not an experimentally measured improvement in research outcomes.
items.streamTitle: Monte Carlo power analysis offered clearer assumptions than AI-generated research participants
items.streamSummary: A November 11 Communications Psychology Comment argues that conventional Monte Carlo power planning exposes effect-size and variance assumptions while synthetic AI respondents bury unverified human-population assumptions in prompts.
items.attribution: Jamie Cummins — Communications Psychology (methodological Comment, November 11)

items.questionAndWhy: Can collective estimates become more accurate if susceptibility to other people's opinions differs across participants? How do network structure and initial bias constrain those improvements?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers analyzed a Friedkin–Johnsen social influence model, rewriting an initially nonconvex susceptibility problem as optimization over social power and then determining which susceptibilities realize that power. They derived analytic cases, realizability conditions and a distributed algorithm.
items.whatTheyFound: Under uniform-sign initial biases the mathematical optimum weighted the least biased agents most strongly. Under mixed-sign biases a different optimal allocation can balance errors. The method provides exact characterizations when its realizability assumptions hold; it uses specified model dynamics rather than observed human interventions.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX expert elicitation or analytical teams, the model suggests testing how initial bias, confidence and network influence affect aggregated judgments. Do not apply theoretically optimal susceptibility weights as human policy until compared with actual group decisions and uncertainty in bias estimates.
items.streamTitle: Opinion-network theory identified which social influence weights reduce collective bias
items.streamSummary: A Friedkin–Johnsen model reformulated susceptibility optimization as social-power allocation and derived conditions for optimal weights. The results are mathematical, not experimentally validated prescriptions for changing human conformity.
items.attribution: Tian, Sheng, Fontan, Wang and Johansson — arXiv preprint (formal social-influence optimization, November 2)

items.questionAndWhy: How do attitudes and adoption behavior coevolve when a population can choose among more than two competing alternatives and later switch choices?
items.whatTheyDid: The researchers formulated a multitechnology adoption–opinion coevolution model with separate physical exposure and social opinion networks. They modeled adoption, dissatisfaction and switching, characterized equilibria and numerically examined finite-horizon opinion-shaping controls.
items.whatTheyFound: The formal model allows multiple alternatives to coexist; with more than two alternatives, equilibrium shares depend on broader competition and opinion states, not just pairwise comparisons. Optimality conditions and numerical extremals are conditional on assumptions. These are theory and simulation results, not measured diffusion or switching in a human population.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX COA comparison, explicitly modeling competing options and abandonment may be preferable to a single adoption variable. This offers a specific structure to test against observed longitudinal audience behavior; using the formal solutions as operationally calibrated forecasts is untested.
items.streamTitle: Coupled adoption and opinion dynamics represented competing alternatives and switching
items.streamSummary: A two-layer MATE model linked exposure, social imitation, dissatisfaction and switching among multiple competing technologies, deriving coexistence equilibria and numerical control solutions. No human intervention forecasts were validated.
items.attribution: Alutto, Dabbene, Fontan, Johansson and Ravazzi — arXiv preprint (formal network-adoption model, November 3)

items.questionAndWhy: Can gaze be measured on practical VR headsets without extensive ground-truth gaze labels? Portable attention measurement needs sensor geometries comparable to actual devices.
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers released VRGaze, containing 2.1 million near-eye infrared images from 68 participants, and trained an unsupervised gaze-representation method. They evaluated personalized calibration, cross-dataset transfer, computational cost and native headset inference.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors report a 1.84-degree mean error after few-shot personal calibration on VRGaze and 5-ms inference on a headset GPU. Cross-dataset person-agnostic error was 7.15 degrees. Accuracy depends on device, dataset and calibration; the work does not infer mental states or establish human learning outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX immersive experiments, this supplies a concrete sensing architecture for time-linked gaze measurements and adaptive interfaces. Gaze location should not be equated with comprehension, belief or intent; operational transfer would require calibration and separate behavioral validation.
items.streamTitle: Near-eye infrared tracking enabled fast, lower-label VR gaze estimates
items.streamSummary: GazeShift released 2.1 million off-axis infrared images from 68 people and reported 1.84-degree calibrated VR gaze error with 5-ms headset inference. This is a sensing benchmark, not evidence of better training or attention.
items.attribution: Shapira, Goldin, Artyomov, Kim, Keller and Zehngut — arXiv preprint, GazeShift/VRGaze (VR sensing dataset, March 8)

items.questionAndWhy: Where in a newsroom's capture-to-publication workflow can cryptographic provenance be lost or mistrusted, and which checks belong at intake versus publication?
items.whatTheyDid: IPTC, CBC/Radio-Canada and Media Cluster Norway developed a standardized workflow map for C2PA metadata from capture and ingestion to editing, packaging and distribution. The framework identifies editorial decisions, signing responsibilities, metadata-loss vulnerabilities and a phased implementation roadmap.
items.whatTheyFound: The framework supplies a common lifecycle vocabulary and templates for auditing provenance handling. It has not established broad newsroom adoption, perfect verification, or reduced audience exposure to false content. Cryptographic provenance is one evidence signal and does not independently certify that a depicted event is true.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX information-integrity analysis, the specific application is logging provenance checks and missing metadata at each media handoff, separately from source credibility and claim verification. This is an operational workflow hypothesis, not a demonstrated influence-mitigation effect.
items.streamTitle: IPTC mapped newsroom checkpoints where media-provenance metadata can fail
items.streamSummary: A media-industry technical framework maps C2PA Content Credentials from capture through newsroom editing and distribution, identifying metadata-loss points and verification checkpoints. It is an implementation design, not a measured decline in misinformation.
items.attribution: Fjellhaug, Armstrong and Quinn — IPTC/IBC technical paper announcement (September 28)
